theorem.statement:
The requested network certificate has a sharp positive boundary case but does not extend to all response-pattern families allowed by \(\mathcal F_{\Gamma}(H)\).  If response is complete in both arms, so that \(M_{ij}(a)=(1,\ldots,1)\) almost surely, then for every finite \(\Gamma\geq1\) the two endpoints are returned by two polynomial-size capacitated minimum-cut calculations, one using \(R\) and one using \(R^c\).  More explicitly, with the fixed complete-response masses \(q_a(c,s)=H_a(c,(1,\ldots,1),s)\), define, for \(Q\in\{R,R^c\}\),
\[
D_{Q,c}=\max_{A\subseteq\mathcal S}
\left\{q_0(c,A)-q_1(c,N_Q(A))\right\}.
\]
Here \(N_Q(A)=\{s_1\in\mathcal S:\text{there is an }s_0\in A\text{ with }(s_0,s_1)\in Q\}\).  Then
\[
U_{\Gamma}=1-\sum_{c\in\mathcal C_{+}}D_{R,c},
\qquad
L_{\Gamma}=\sum_{c\in\mathcal C_{+}}D_{R^c,c}.
\]
Each calculation returns an endpoint-attaining response-stratum-preserving coupling and a collection of maximizing cut sets \(A_c\).  The disjoint stratum networks may be joined at a common source and sink, so each endpoint requires one maximum-flow/minimum-cut problem.  For rational \(H_a\), integer scaling and residual matching return rational couplings and integral cuts.

This conclusion cannot be promoted to the general missing-pattern model by treating \(\mathfrak H_R\) as a network matrix or balanced hypergraph.  Already with one stratum, \(d=3\), binary outcomes, \(\Gamma=1\), and the three singleton-coordinate response patterns of the projection-obstruction lemma, the eliminated arm-completion incidence contains an odd-cycle submatrix of determinant minus two and has a fractional vertex on the observed-law integer lattice.  Hence that signed incidence system is neither balanced nor a network matrix up to row and column permutations and sign changes.  This is a non-representability frontier for the direct incidence formulation: complete response admits the two transparent cut certificates, whereas the permitted three-way singleton-pattern design can require the generic linear-program certificates from the joint sharpness theorem.  The obstruction does not rule out an unrelated extended formulation with auxiliary variables for a particular relation or a special intermediate pattern family.
theorem.proof_tex:
Under complete response, the complete-response reduction gives, for every finite \(\Gamma\geq1\),
\[
q_a(c,s)=H_a(c,(1,\ldots,1),s),
\qquad
\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}q_a(c,s)=\kappa(c),
\]
and it makes all sensitivity inequalities redundant.  Thus the only free variables in \(\mathcal F_{\Gamma}(H)\) are, separately for each \(c\in\mathcal C_{+}\), couplings with row masses \(q_0(c,\cdot)\) and column masses \(q_1(c,\cdot)\).

Fix a stratum \(c\) and apply the finite-relation capacity lemma with
\[
T=\mathcal S,
\qquad
\mu_0(s)=q_0(c,s),
\qquad
\mu_1(s)=q_1(c,s),
\qquad
w=\kappa(c).
\]
For \(Q=R\), the maximum attainable strict-benefit mass in this stratum is
\[
\kappa(c)-D_{R,c}.
\]
The constraints do not connect different positive-mass strata.  Maximizing separately and using
\[
\sum_{c\in\mathcal C_{+}}\kappa(c)=1
\]
therefore gives
\[
\max_{x\in\mathcal F_{\Gamma}(H)}c_R^{\mathsf T}x
=\sum_{c\in\mathcal C_{+}}\{\kappa(c)-D_{R,c}\}
=1-\sum_{c\in\mathcal C_{+}}D_{R,c}.
\]
By the definition of the sharp endpoint, this is \(U_{\Gamma}\).

Apply the same lemma with \(Q=R^c\).  The largest attainable nonbenefit mass is
\[
\sum_{c\in\mathcal C_{+}}\{\kappa(c)-D_{R^c,c}\}
=1-\sum_{c\in\mathcal C_{+}}D_{R^c,c}.
\]
Since every coupling has total mass one and \(R\) and \(R^c\) partition \(\mathcal S\times\mathcal S\), minimizing benefit is the same as maximizing nonbenefit.  Hence
\[
L_{\Gamma}=1-\left\{1-\sum_{c\in\mathcal C_{+}}D_{R^c,c}\right\}
=\sum_{c\in\mathcal C_{+}}D_{R^c,c}.
\]

The constructive part of the lemma gives the algorithms.  For the upper endpoint, use a source, left vertices \((c,s_0)\), right vertices \((c,s_1)\), and a sink.  Give the source edge capacity \(q_0(c,s_0)\), the sink edge capacity \(q_1(c,s_1)\), and include an internal edge of capacity two exactly when \((s_0,s_1)\in R\).  There are no internal edges between different strata.  A maximum flow and its residual-reachability cut decompose over \(c\), return the maximizing sets \(A_c\), and have total value \(U_{\Gamma}\).  Residual row and column matching within each stratum completes the flow to a coupling \(\pi_U\) whose strict-benefit mass is \(U_{\Gamma}\).  Replacing \(R\) by \(R^c\) returns a coupling maximizing nonbenefit; the same coupling, denoted \(\pi_L\), has strict-benefit mass \(L_{\Gamma}\).  Thus there are exactly two flow calculations, one per endpoint.  Each graph has
\[
2+2|\mathcal C_{+}||\mathcal S|
\]
vertices and at most
\[
2|\mathcal C_{+}||\mathcal S|
+|\mathcal C_{+}||\mathcal S|^2
\]
edges.  Thus this is a polynomial-size maximum-flow problem; standard polynomial-time maximum-flow algorithms apply to rational inputs.  The rational-lattice assertion follows from the last part of the finite-relation capacity lemma.  The joint observed-data sharpness theorem then identifies these attained optimization values with the causal identified-set endpoints, rather than merely with outer bounds.

It remains to show why this construction is not valid for every allowed response family.  The projection-obstruction lemma supplies an admissible member of the frozen model with three binary coordinates, three singleton-coordinate response patterns, and \(\Gamma=1\).  Its eliminated projection incidence contains a three-by-three odd-cycle matrix with determinant minus two, is not balanced, is not totally unimodular, and has a fractional arm-completion vertex after scaling by the least common denominator of \(H_a\).  A directed network matrix is totally unimodular, while row and column permutations and sign changes preserve absolute determinants.  Therefore the direct signed incidence system \(\mathfrak H_R\) for that response family cannot have the proposed network-matrix or balanced-hypergraph representation.  The generic primal and dual linear programs in the joint sharpness theorem remain valid, but their certificates need not be cuts.  Combining the constructive complete-response argument with this explicit admissible obstruction proves the stated frontier and the claimed qualification concerning unrelated extended formulations.

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(T\) be a finite set, let \(\mu_0\) and \(\mu_1\) be nonnegative measures on \(T\) having the same total mass \(w\), and let \(Q\subseteq T\times T\).  Put
\[
\Pi(\mu_0,\mu_1)
=\left\{\rho\geq 0:
  \sum_y\rho(x,y)=\mu_0(x),\ 
  \sum_x\rho(x,y)=\mu_1(y)\right\},
\]
\[
N_Q(A)=\{y\in T:\text{there is an }x\in A\text{ with }(x,y)\in Q\},
\qquad
D_Q=\max_{A\subseteq T}\{\mu_0(A)-\mu_1(N_Q(A))\}.
\]
Then
\[
\max_{\rho\in\Pi(\mu_0,\mu_1)}\rho(Q)=w-D_Q.
\]
The maximum is attained.  A capacitated bipartite maximum-flow calculation returns both an attaining coupling and a set \(A\) attaining \(D_Q\).  If \(\mu_0\) and \(\mu_1\) are rational, scaling by a common denominator and using integral augmentations followed by integral residual matching returns a coupling on the same rational lattice.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Construct a directed graph with source \(o\), sink \(t\), a left copy of \(T\), and a right copy of \(T\).  Give \(o\to x\) capacity \(\mu_0(x)\), give \(y\to t\) capacity \(\mu_1(y)\), and give \(x\to y\) capacity \(w+1\) exactly when \((x,y)\in Q\).  The zero flow is feasible, and the finite-dimensional feasible-flow polytope is compact, so a maximum flow \(f\) exists.

Here is a self-contained cut argument.  If the residual graph of \(f\) contained a directed path from \(o\) to \(t\), the minimum residual capacity along that finite path would be positive, and augmenting by this amount would strictly increase the flow.  Thus no such path exists.  Let \(S_f\) be the vertices reachable from \(o\) in the residual graph.  Every original edge leaving \(S_f\) is saturated and every original edge entering \(S_f\) carries zero flow.  Summing flow conservation over the vertices in \(S_f\setminus\{o\}\) therefore shows that the value of \(f\) equals the capacity of the cut \((S_f,S_f^c)\).  Conversely, summing conservation over the source side of any cut shows that every feasible-flow value is at most that cut's capacity.  Hence \(f\) and its residual-reachability cut are respectively a maximum flow and a minimum cut.

The cut that places only \(o\) on the source side has capacity \(w\).  Since every internal edge has capacity \(w+1\), no minimum cut crosses an internal edge.  If \(A\) is the set of left vertices on the source side, every member of \(N_Q(A)\) is consequently on the source side.  Deleting from the source side any right vertex outside \(N_Q(A)\) cannot increase the cut capacity.  Thus a minimum cut has capacity
\[
\min_{A\subseteq T}
\{\mu_0(T\setminus A)+\mu_1(N_Q(A))\}
=w-\max_{A\subseteq T}
\{\mu_0(A)-\mu_1(N_Q(A))\}
=w-D_Q.
\]
The flow on the internal edges is a \(Q\)-supported subcoupling with mass \(w-D_Q\).  Define its residual row and column masses by
\[
r(x)=\mu_0(x)-\sum_y f(x,y),
\qquad
c(y)=\mu_1(y)-\sum_x f(x,y).
\]
Flow conservation gives
\[
\sum_xr(x)=\sum_yc(y)=D_Q.
\]
If \(r(x)>0\), \(c(y)>0\), and \((x,y)\in Q\), then \(o\to x\to y\to t\) is a residual augmenting path: the first and last edges have positive residual capacity, while the internal edge has residual capacity at least \((w+1)-w>0\).  This contradicts maximality.  Therefore
\[
\operatorname{supp}(r)\times\operatorname{supp}(c)\subseteq Q^c.
\]
When \(D_Q>0\), set
\[
\rho_Q(x,y)=f(x,y)+\frac{r(x)c(y)}{D_Q};
\]
when \(D_Q=0\), set \(\rho_Q=f\).  In either case \(\rho_Q\in\Pi(\mu_0,\mu_1)\), and the added mass lies in \(Q^c\), so
\[
\rho_Q(Q)=w-D_Q.
\]
For the reverse inequality, for every \(\rho\in\Pi(\mu_0,\mu_1)\) and every \(A\subseteq T\), every \(Q\)-cell either has its left endpoint outside \(A\) or its right endpoint in \(N_Q(A)\).  Hence
\[
\rho(Q)
\leq \mu_0(T\setminus A)+\mu_1(N_Q(A))
=w-\{\mu_0(A)-\mu_1(N_Q(A))\}.
\]
Minimizing the right side over \(A\) proves the claimed equality and attainment.

Finally, suppose a positive integer \(D\) makes \(D\mu_0\) and \(D\mu_1\) integer valued.  After scaling, use internal capacity \(Dw+1\).  Starting from zero, an augmenting-path algorithm always augments by a positive integer.  Its value is bounded by the integer \(Dw\), so it terminates at an integral maximum flow.  The residual row and column masses are integers.  Repeatedly send the smaller of a positive residual row mass and a positive residual column mass between such a pair.  The support argument above ensures that every selected pair lies in \(Q^c\), and each step exhausts a row or a column.  This produces an integral residual matching.  Dividing by \(D\) gives the asserted rational coupling and completes the proof.

added_lemmas.statement:
There is an admissible one-stratum observed law \(H_a\) with \(d=3\), \(\mathcal S=\{0,1\}^3\), and \(\Gamma=1\) for which the projection of \(\mathcal F_{\Gamma}(H)\) onto the arm-completion coordinates \(q_a\) has an incidence matrix containing the odd-cycle matrix
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
1&1&0\\
1&0&1\\
0&1&1
\end{pmatrix},
\]
whose determinant has absolute value two.  The matrix is therefore neither balanced nor totally unimodular and cannot be a directed network matrix up to row and column permutations and sign changes.  Moreover, although the observed masses have least common denominator six, the arm-completion polytope has a vertex whose four positive \(q_a\)-coordinates become \(3/2\) after multiplication by six.  Thus rational observed masses do not give the natural missing-pattern incidence system the integral-lattice certificate enjoyed by a flow network.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Take one response stratum \(c\) with \(\kappa(c)=1\), take \(d=3\), and take \(\mathcal S=\{0,1\}^3\).  Let the only positive-probability response patterns be
\[
m^{(1)}=(1,0,0),\qquad
m^{(2)}=(0,1,0),\qquad
m^{(3)}=(0,0,1).
\]
For both arms, specify the observed law by
\[
H_a(c,m^{(k)},z)=\frac16
\quad
\text{for }a\in\{0,1\},\ k\in\{1,2,3\},\ z\in\{0,1\},
\]
and set all other observed-pattern masses to zero.  Summing over \(z\) gives
\[
r_a(m^{(k)}\mid c)=\frac13.
\]
At \(\Gamma=1\), the two sensitivity inequalities in the definition of \(\mathcal F_{\Gamma}(H)\) coincide.  Consequently,
\[
\lambda_a(c,s,m^{(k)})=\frac13q_a(c,s),
\]
whereas every zero-frequency pattern has zero \(\lambda_a\)-mass.  The projection equations are therefore equivalent to
\[
\sum_{s:s_k=z}q_a(c,s)=\frac12
\quad
\text{for }k\in\{1,2,3\},\ z\in\{0,1\}.
\]
Together with total mass one, it is enough to retain the three equations with \(z=1\).

Consider the completion
\[
q^{\star}(000)=q^{\star}(110)=q^{\star}(101)=q^{\star}(011)=\frac14,
\qquad
q^{\star}(s)=0\quad\text{otherwise}.
\]
It satisfies every displayed marginal equation.  On its four-element support, the total-mass row followed by the three coordinate-one rows gives the coefficient matrix
\[
B=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&1&1&1\\
0&1&1&0\\
0&1&0&1\\
0&0&1&1
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\det(B)=-2.
\]
The equations \(Bx=(1,1/2,1/2,1/2)^{\mathsf T}\) have the unique solution
\[
x=(1/4,1/4,1/4,1/4)^{\mathsf T}.
\]
After imposing zero on the other four nonnegative coordinates, this uniqueness proves that \(q^{\star}\) is a vertex of the arm-completion polytope.

Restricting the last three rows to the columns \(110,101,011\) produces
\[
C=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&1&0\\
1&0&1\\
0&1&1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Every row and column of \(C\) contains exactly two ones, its order is odd, and \(\det(C)=-2\).  By the defining forbidden-submatrix condition for a balanced zero-one matrix, the projection incidence matrix is not balanced.  The determinant also shows directly that it is not totally unimodular.

For completeness, the node-arc incidence matrix of a directed graph is totally unimodular: for any square submatrix, expansion applies if a column has at most one nonzero entry, while if every column has two nonzero entries, one \(+1\) and one \(-1\), the rows are linearly dependent and the determinant is zero.  The same determinant property holds for a directed network matrix, since each of its minors is, up to sign, a minor obtained by replacing columns of a nonsingular tree-incidence basis.  Row or column permutations and sign changes preserve absolute determinants.  The displayed determinant of absolute value two therefore rules out such a network representation of this incidence system.

The observed masses are zero or \(1/6\), so their least common denominator is six, but
\[
6q^{\star}(s)=\frac32
\]
on each positive cell.  Hence the polytope is not integral on the observed-law lattice.  Finally, this is a genuine feasible observed law, not merely an isolated arm calculation: take the displayed completion in both arms, set \(\lambda_a=q^{\star}/3\) on the three positive patterns, and use the product coupling
\[
\pi(c,s_0,s_1)=q^{\star}(s_0)q^{\star}(s_1).
\]
All projection, completion, sensitivity, and coupling equations in \(\mathcal F_1(H)\) then hold.  This proves the claimed obstruction.
